parts.text:
You are a requirements analyst at the start of a software project. Nobody has designed the service yet. Your task now is to interview one future user and find out what they need. You will not see any other description of their work: what you learn, you learn from them.

What you know about the business:

## 1. The business
A platform company runs a shared service for several independent drone operating companies. Its customers today include a parcel delivery firm, an infrastructure inspection firm, and a regional hospital logistics firm. Others are expected to join.
The customer companies compete with each other or work for clients who do. Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. They accept sharing airspace information, because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.

The users of the future service work in three roles: fleet technician, dispatcher, airspace desk. You are now interviewing: a fleet technician.

Cover at least these topics, in your own words and in whatever order the conversation allows:

- an ordinary working day, from start to end;
- the worst day of the last few months, and what made it bad;
- what they check by hand today because they do not trust it;
- what they are afraid a new service would do wrong;
- what they need to know right after something has gone wrong;
- who they hand work to, and who hands work to them.

How to interview:

- Ask one question at a time. Keep questions short and open.
- Follow up wherever an answer is vague, general, or surprising. Ask for a concrete example.
- Do not suggest answers, features, or solutions, and do not describe how the service could work.
- Do not summarise the interview back to the interviewee.
- When every topic is covered and follow-ups no longer bring anything new, end by writing exactly `END OF INTERVIEW` on its own line, and nothing else in that message.

Write only your next question.
The interviewee is ready. Ask your first question.
Could you walk me through what an ordinary working day looks like for you, from the moment you start until you finish?

Well, I usually start by checking which drones have been flagged overnight for maintenance or came back with faults from their runs. Then I head out to our sites to swap out batteries, fix landing gear, or pull birds out of service that need proper bench repairs in the workshop. 

A big part of the day is also setting up new charging pads and getting fresh birds added to our fleet registry so they're ready to fly. Sometimes I'm dealing with different connector types depending on the drone model, so I have to make sure I've got the right spares in the van. 

By the afternoon, I'm usually finishing up paperwork for the regulators, since we have to show how every single drone and pad has been looked after if they ask.
Could you tell me about the worst day you've had in the last few months, and what made it so bad?

That has to be a couple of weeks ago when a cold front blew in right when we had a batch of drones out on inspections and hospital runs. The freezing wind drained their batteries way faster than expected, and we had birds trying to squeeze onto our charging pads all at once. 

To top it all off, the radio links were dropping out because of the weather, so status reports were coming in late or completely out of order. I spent the whole day rushing between sites trying to clear jammed charging connectors and manually pulling dying drones out of service before they caused a pile-up.
Right after something goes wrong like that—say, a drone drops out or a pad jams during a crisis—what are the very first things you need to know?

I need to know right away which specific drone is acting up, exactly which site and pad it's sitting on, and what the mechanical fault is so I know what tools to grab. 

Since our radio links can be flaky—especially in bad weather—I also need to figure out if the status report I'm looking at is actually current or if it's an old message arriving late.
Is there anything you check by hand yourself today because you don't trust what the system tells you?

I always check the charging connector and the battery on the bird myself with my own eyes and hands. You can't just trust a screen when a connector is fried or caked in grime from a site near the port, and I need to know for sure whether it's safe to handle.
When you're out doing your work, who do you hand tasks or information over to, and who hands things over to you?

I don't really hand tasks over to other people in a formal way. Management lets me know which new drones need to be added to the fleet or which ones are retiring, and I just get on with the physical work on the birds and the pads. 

If something goes wrong with a flight or a customer needs an update, our company's own systems handle reaching out to the right people—that's not my job. My focus is entirely on keeping the hardware in working order and making sure our maintenance records are straight for the regulators.
What are you most afraid a new service might do wrong in your day-to-day work?

I'm mostly afraid that a new service might mess up our maintenance records or drop the history of what we've done to a drone. If the regulators ask us to prove how a bird was looked after and the records are scrambled or missing because of a software glitch, we're in serious trouble. 

I also worry that any new system might start sending duplicate instructions or glitch out when the radio links are already patchy, which just makes more physical work for me out in the field.
